intro: Your weakest topics are at the top, based on your own mocks, and the order updates after every mock you finish. Start each topic with its **big idea** and the worked example, then read the rules and the traps.

items.name: Arc (piece of the edge)
items.note: use the angle at the center

items.name: Square inside a circle
items.note: its diagonal is the circle's width, $2r$

items.name: Chord
items.note: $d$ = distance from the center to the chord

items.name: Area
items.note: any side can be the base

items.name: Third side
items.note: two sides always beat the third

items.name: Perpendicular slope
items.note: flip it and change the sign

formats.title: Quantitative Comparison
rules: Your job is to try to **break** it. Try two very different numbers. If the winner changes, the answer is (D).
Good numbers to try: $0$, $1$, $-1$, $\frac12$, a big number, and both ends of any allowed range.
No letters, just numbers? Then it can't be (D). Just work it out.
Picture 'not drawn to scale' shapes stretched or squished in every way the facts allow.

formats.title: Multiple choice, one answer
rules: Look at the answers first. They tell you how exact you need to be.
Stuck setting it up? Try the middle answer in the question and see if it's too big or too small.
No numbers given? Make some up (like 100 for percents).
The wrong answers are the usual mistakes. Getting one of them doesn't prove you're right.

formats.title: Select all that apply
rules: All or nothing: no partial credit. Judge each choice yes/no on its own.
First find the rule (a range, 'multiples of 47', 'odd numbers from 5 to 65'), then test every choice against it, including **both ends**.
Picking every choice is almost never right. Look for the one built to fail.

formats.title: Numeric Entry
rules: There are no choices to catch a mistake, so reread the last sentence and **underline what they're asking for**.
Plug your answer back into the question to check it.
Fractions don't need simplifying. Negative answers are allowed.

formats.title: Charts & tables
rules: Read the title, labels and units before you start.
Estimate first. The answers are often far apart.
For 'percent of' and 'percent more than', check what you're dividing by.

pacing: About **1:45 per question**: 12 questions in 21 minutes, then 15 in 26.
If you're at **2:30** with no plan, guess, mark it, and move on. You can come back.
Do the easy ones first; come back to marked ones with the time you saved.
Practice with the timer on (exam mode), so your score is real.
A 170 means 0–2 mistakes. The easiest points to win back are comparison traps and misreading the question.

sections.title: Circles & shapes inside circles
sections.idea: Almost every circle problem is a **right triangle** in disguise. Draw a line from the center to a point on the circle: that's the radius, and it's usually the long side of a right triangle.

example.q: A square has all four corners on a circle of radius 5. What is the area of the square?
steps: The square's diagonal (corner to corner) goes straight across the circle, so the diagonal is $2\times5=10$.
A square with diagonal $d$ has area $\frac{d^2}{2}$.
Area $=\frac{100}{2}=50$. (Quick check with the shortcut: $2r^2=2\times25=50$.)

facts: **Square inside a circle:** the diagonal = the circle's width ($2r$). Area $=2r^2$.
**Circle inside a square:** the circle touches all four sides, so the side $=2r$. Area $=4r^2$.
Square in a circle in a square: each square is exactly **half** the one around it.
**Square in a half-circle** (sitting on the flat side): area $=\frac45r^2$. Its top corners are half a side across and one full side up from the center, so $\left(\frac s2\right)^2+s^2=r^2$.
**Chord** = a straight line across the circle. A line from the center that meets it at a right angle cuts it exactly **in half**.
**Arc** = part of the edge. Arc $=\frac{\text{center angle}}{360}\times2\pi r$.
A line that just touches the circle (a tangent) makes a right angle with the radius.
tricks: Stuck? Draw the radius to every point that's on the circle and look for the right triangle.
Two chords on **opposite sides** of the center: their distances from the center **add up** to the gap between them.
If half the chord ÷ radius $=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, the half-angle is $60^\circ$, so the full center angle is $120^\circ$.
traps: Using the diameter as the square's **side**. It's the square's **diagonal** that equals the diameter.
Using the half-angle as the center angle. Your arc comes out half as long as it should.
Using the whole chord in the triangle. Always use **half** the chord.

sections.title: Triangles
sections.idea: Learn two special triangles by heart. Most hard triangle questions are one of them in disguise; you just have to **cut the shape** the right way.

example.q: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B=30^\circ$ and side $BC=8$. How long is the height from $C$ straight down to side $AB$?
steps: Drop the height from $C$. On the $B$ side you get a 30-60-90 triangle, and $BC=8$ is its longest side.
In a 30-60-90 triangle, the side across from $30^\circ$ is **half** the longest side.
The height is across from the $30^\circ$ angle, so it is $\frac82=4$.

facts: **45-45-90** (half a square): sides $1:1:\sqrt2$. The long side = short side $\times\sqrt2$.
**30-60-90** (half an equilateral triangle): sides $1:\sqrt3:2$. The shortest side is across from $30^\circ$, and the longest is twice that.
**Area** $=\frac12\times$ base $\times$ height, and **any** side can be the base. So the height to a side $=\frac{2\times\text{area}}{\text{that side}}$.
Any two sides add up to **more** than the third side.
The biggest angle is across from the longest side.
Whole-number right triangles to know: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and their multiples like 6-8-10.
tricks: Not a right triangle? **Drop a height** to split it into two special right triangles.
'Not drawn to scale' means don't trust your eyes. Imagine stretching the shape every way the facts still allow.
traps: Assuming an angle is $90^\circ$ just because it looks like one.
Assuming a line hits the middle, or is a height, when the question never says so.
Forgetting the $\frac12$ in the area.

sections.title: Lines & graphs
sections.idea: Slope just means 'how far **up** for each step **right**'. Most line questions come down to slope.

example.q: A line goes through $(1, 6)$ and is perpendicular to a line with slope $\frac23$. Where does it cross the $x$-axis?
steps: Perpendicular slope: flip the fraction and change the sign. $\frac23\to-\frac32$.
$-\frac32$ means every 2 steps right, the line drops 3.
To get from $y=6$ down to $y=0$ it drops 6. That takes $2\times2=4$ steps right.
$x=1+4=5$, so it crosses at $(5, 0)$.

facts: Slope $=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.
For a line written as $Ax+By=C$, the slope is $-\frac AB$.
**Perpendicular** lines (meeting at a right angle): flip the fraction **and** change the sign.
**Parallel** lines have the **same** slope.
Crossing the $x$-axis means $y=0$. Crossing the $y$-axis means $x=0$.
Midpoint: average the $x$'s, average the $y$'s.
tricks: Sketch it quickly. Answers on the wrong side of an axis can be crossed off right away.
Square from two opposite corners: find the middle point. Walk from the middle to one corner (say 3 right, 2 up). Turn that walk a quarter turn (2 left, 3 up) to find another corner.
traps: Changing the sign but forgetting to flip the fraction, or flipping it without changing the sign.
Answering where the line crosses the $y$-axis when they asked about the $x$-axis.
Calling a rectangle a square without checking that its sides are equal.

sections.title: Polygons, area & volume
sections.idea: Walk all the way around any shape and you turn one full circle, so the outside angles **always add up to $360^\circ$**. That one fact solves most polygon angle questions.

example.q: Each inside angle of a regular polygon is $140^\circ$. How many diagonals does it have?
steps: Inside + outside angle make a straight line, so the outside angle is $180-140=40^\circ$.
All outside angles add to $360^\circ$, so it has $\frac{360}{40}=9$ sides.
Diagonals $=\frac{9\times(9-3)}{2}=\frac{54}{2}=27$.

facts: Outside angles add to $360^\circ$. In a regular shape (all sides equal), each one is $\frac{360}{n}$.
Inside angle + outside angle $=180^\circ$.
All inside angles add to $(n-2)\times180^\circ$: triangle 180, square 360, pentagon 540.
Diagonals $=\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$. Each corner connects to $n-3$ others, and every diagonal gets counted twice.
Rectangles with the same diagonal: the **square** has the biggest perimeter. The skinnier the rectangle, the smaller the perimeter.
Box volume = length × width × height. Cylinder volume $=\pi r^2\times$ height.
tricks: 'Inside angle is 5 times the outside angle': outside + 5 × outside $=180$, so outside $=30^\circ$ and there are $\frac{360}{30}=12$ sides.
'Which could be' questions: find the **smallest and largest** possible values first, then check each choice.
traps: Assuming the sides are whole numbers when the question never says so.
Giving the number of sides when they asked for diagonals.
Forgetting to divide $n(n-3)$ by 2.

sections.title: Counting & probability
sections.idea: Counting is **filling slots**. Count the choices for each slot and multiply, and always fill the **pickiest** slot first.

example.q: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a line if Sam and Tia must stand next to each other?
steps: Tape Sam and Tia together into one block. Now you're lining up 4 things: $4!=24$ ways.
Inside the block they can be Sam-Tia or Tia-Sam: $\times2$.
$24\times2=48$ ways.

facts: Lining up $n$ different things: $n!$ ways ($4!=4\times3\times2\times1=24$).
Picking a group where order doesn't matter: $\binom nk$, read '$n$ choose $k$'. $\binom52=10$.
Some things the same? Divide out the repeats: AABB has $\frac{4!}{2!\,2!}=6$ orders.
**Must be together:** tape them into a block, line up the blocks, then $\times2$ because the two can swap.
**Must NOT be together:** all the ways − the ways they're together.
Probability $=\frac{\text{good outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}$. P(at least one) $=1-$ P(none).
tricks: **Pickiest first.** If Ann can't sit at either end of 8 seats, give Ann her 6 choices before anyone else sits.
If one person's choice changes how many choices the next person has, split it into cases, or count the opposite and subtract.
'Digits in decreasing order' means the order is already decided. You're only **choosing** the digits, so use $\binom nk$.
Not sure? Try a tiny version (3 people) and list every possibility to check your method.
traps: Multiplying as if the choices don't affect each other when they do.
Forgetting the $\times2$ for the two people in a block swapping places.
In 'none of A, B or C' problems, subtracting the overlaps but forgetting to add the triple overlap back.

sections.title: Overlapping groups & max/min
sections.idea: When people are in two groups, the ones in **both** get counted twice. Every group formula is just fixing that double count.

example.q: Of 40 students, 25 play soccer and 22 play basketball. What is the fewest number who could play both?
steps: $25+22=47$, but there are only 40 students.
So at least $47-40=7$ students were counted twice.
The fewest who play both is **7** (that's when every student plays at least one).

facts: Total $=A+B-$ both $+$ neither.
Exactly one group $=A+B-2\times$ both. (Take the 'both' people out of each group.)
'Both' can't be bigger than the smaller group, and can't be smaller than $A+B-$ total.
tricks: Max or min question? First find the smallest and biggest possible 'both', then plug those in.
Draw a 2×2 table (in A / not in A by in B / not in B). Fill what you know; the rest falls out.
To make one thing as **big** as possible, make everything else as **small** as allowed.
traps: Assuming nobody is in both groups when the numbers don't allow it.
Assuming everyone is in at least one group.
In 'which could be' questions, checking odd/even but forgetting the smallest and largest limits.

sections.title: Remainders, factors & powers
sections.idea: Remainders and last digits **repeat in a pattern**. Find the pattern with the first few powers, and you never have to work out a huge number.

example.q: What is the last digit of $7^{43}$?
steps: Last digits of $7^1, 7^2, 7^3, 7^4$: 7, 9, 3, 1. Then it starts over, so the pattern repeats every 4.
$43=40+3$. The 40 is ten full rounds, so we land on the **3rd** spot.
The 3rd spot is **3**.

facts: You can swap a number for its remainder. 17 leaves 1 when divided by 8, so $17^{50}$ leaves $1^{50}=1$.
Last digits repeat: 2, 3, 7, 8 every 4 powers; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 never change.
**Each number has its own pattern length.** Don't assume two bases repeat at the same speed.
Any odd number squared leaves remainder 1 when divided by 8 ($9$, $25$, $49$…).
Counting factors: write $n=2^a\times3^b\times\ldots$, then the count is $(a+1)(b+1)\cdots$. $12=2^2\times3$ has $3\times2=6$ factors.
Only perfect squares have an odd number of factors.
tricks: Write out the first few remainders until they repeat, then jump ahead using the pattern length.
'$k$ leaves remainder 5 when divided by 6'? Test real numbers: $k=5$, then $k=11$.
Comparing factor counts? Test 1, a prime, a prime power **and** a number made of several primes, like 30.
traps: Assuming two different bases repeat at the same speed.
Testing only primes and missing the case that flips the answer.

sections.title: Algebra & inequalities
sections.idea: An inequality works like an equation with **one extra rule**: multiply or divide by a negative and you must flip the sign.

steps: $|x-1|$ is the distance from $x$ to 1, so this says: distance to 1 + distance to 5 is at most 6.
Anywhere between 1 and 5 the total is 4. Each step outside adds 2.
So you can go 1 step past each end: $0\le x\le6$.

facts: Multiply or divide by a negative → **flip** the $<$ or $>$.
$|x-a|$ means 'how far $x$ is from $a$ on the number line'.
If $x+\frac1x=s$, squaring both sides gives $x^2+\frac1{x^2}=s^2-2$.
For $x^2+bx+c=0$, the two answers **add** to $-b$ and **multiply** to $c$.
Two lines with the same slope never meet: **no solution**. If they're the exact same line: **infinitely many**.
tricks: Two inequalities at once? Solve each, draw both on a number line, and keep the overlap.
Getting $k^2=36$? Try **both** $6$ and $-6$ back in the question.
Can't solve it? Plug in the answer choices.
traps: Forgetting to flip the sign.
Using an endpoint that isn't allowed. With $<$, the endpoint itself is out.
Choosing the value that makes the two lines the **same** when they asked for 'no solution'.
Sign mix-up: the answers add to $-b$, not $b$.

sections.title: Ratios, percents & word problems
sections.idea: Find the thing that **doesn't change** and build your equation around it.

example.q: A club's ratio of boys to girls is $2:3$. After 10 boys join, the ratio is $1:1$. How many people were in the club before?
steps: The girls don't change. Call them $3k$; the boys were $2k$.
After: boys $2k+10$ = girls $3k$, so $k=10$.
Before: $2k+3k=5k=$ **50** people. (They asked for 'before', not after.)

facts: A ratio of $3:5$ means the amounts are $3k$ and $5k$. The total, $8k$, is a multiple of 8.
Joining two ratios: make the shared item match. A:B $=2:3$ and B:C $=4:5$. Make B 12: A:B:C $=8:12:15$.
'X is what percent **more than** Y': divide the difference by Y, the number after 'than'.
Up $p\%$ means multiply by $1+\frac p{100}$. Up 25% = $\times1.25$. Up 700% = $\times8$, **not** $\times7$.
Growing the same percent every year means **multiplying** by the same number every year. $\times8$ over 3 periods is $\times2$ each time, because $2\times2\times2=8$.
Working together: **add the rates**. A takes 3 hours ($\frac13$ of the job per hour) and B takes 6 ($\frac16$ per hour). Together: $\frac13+\frac16=\frac12$ per hour, so 2 hours.
tricks: Let one letter stand for the smallest amount and write everything else using it.
Before you answer, reread the last sentence and **underline what they're asking for**.
Plug your answer back into the story to check.
traps: Giving a middle step (one person's share) instead of what they asked for (the total).
Splitting growth evenly: up 700% over 3 periods is **not** 233% each time.
Dividing by the wrong number in 'percent more than' questions.

sections.title: Averages, spread & charts
sections.idea: When you combine groups, **group size matters**: a big group pulls the average toward itself.

example.q: Class A has 10 students averaging 80. Class B has 30 students averaging 60. What is the average of all 40?
steps: Totals: $10\times80=800$ and $30\times60=1800$.
Not 70! The bigger class pulls the average toward 60.

facts: Combining groups: add all the totals, then divide by everyone. Don't just average the averages.
Bell curve: about 68% are within 1 standard deviation (SD) of the middle, and 95% within 2.
So about **16%** are more than 1 SD **above** the middle, and about **2.5%** are more than 2 SD above.
SD measures how spread out the numbers are. Add the same amount to every number and the spread stays the same.
Median = the middle number once they're sorted. With an even count, average the two middle ones.
Q1 = middle of the lower half, Q3 = middle of the upper half. IQR = Q3 − Q1.
tricks: Groups with different spreads? Work out how many SDs the cutoff is **for each group separately**.
Charts: read the title, labels and units first. Estimate before you calculate.
traps: Averaging the averages.
Using 32% (both tails of the curve) when they only asked about one side.
Thinking new numbers at the far ends can't change the quartiles. They change which numbers sit in the middle of each half.

sections.title: Comparison number sense
sections.idea: In comparison questions, try to **break** the comparison. If two different numbers give different winners, the answer is (D).

steps: Try $x=\frac12$: A $=\frac14$, B $=\frac12$. B wins.
Try $x=-\frac12$: A $=\frac14$, B $=-\frac12$. A wins.
Different winners, so the answer is **(D)**.

facts: Between 0 and 1, squaring makes a number **smaller**: $\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14$. Above 1, it makes it bigger.
For a number between 0 and 1, $\frac1x$ is bigger than 1.
$0.999\ldots$ (repeating forever) is **exactly** 1.
A repeating decimal like $0.\overline{27}$ equals $\frac{27}{99}$.
tricks: Always try at least two numbers: $0$, $1$, $-1$, $\frac12$, a negative, a big number, and both ends of the allowed range.
Only numbers, no letters? Then it can't be (D). Just work it out.
Simplify by doing the same thing to both sides, but only multiply by numbers you know are positive.
traps: Trying only one number and stopping.
Answering in 20 seconds without trying a second number.
